sources.title: Nvidia stops AI GPU shipments to Southeast Asia amid purported China cloud access ban, report claims

stories.headline: Nvidia halts AI server shipments to Southeast Asia, report says
stories.dek: Data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia face a 90-day scramble for US export licenses as Washington targets Chinese cloud access.
stories.body:
Nvidia has reportedly told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping AI servers to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. According to the Financial Times, as reported by Tom's Hardware, Dell, Supermicro and other firms that build servers around Nvidia AI GPUs have told customers in the four countries that the chipmaker has forbidden them to ship their orders.

The halt follows a US move to close a loophole that let Chinese AI companies rent compute from data centers outside China equipped with advanced American chips. Under the new export rules, cloud providers have 90 days to apply for an export license and prove that their customers do not include restricted entities.

The US has banned exports of advanced AI chips to China since 2022. President Trump allowed Nvidia to export H100 GPUs to China in December 2025, but buyers still need an import license from the Commerce Department, and the White House collects a 25 percent fee on every chip. That pushed many Chinese AI labs to rent compute abroad, mostly in Southeast Asia, a four- to six-hour flight from Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Shanghai. Some firms have also looked as far as Europe.

The rollout appears messy. One cloud provider executive told the Financial Times there are no clear instructions for applying. "There's this new rule but no guidance on execution," they said. "No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It's causing sheer chaos in the region."

The financial fallout is already visible, according to the report. Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud company with a deal to provide compute to ByteDance, is reportedly losing financing as bankers have stopped issuing $500 million in credit while shipments remain in doubt. ByteDance could also drop out of the arrangement if it cannot reach the Nvidia chips many AI labs still prefer for training.

It remains unclear whether Nvidia's order is permanent or temporary. Neither the length of the pause nor how licenses will be granted has been spelled out.
key_points: Nvidia reportedly ordered partners to stop AI server shipments to four countries
Cloud providers get 90 days to obtain US export licenses
Singapore's Aolani reportedly loses $500 million in credit tied to ByteDance deal
Unclear whether the halt is temporary or permanent
stories.why_it_matters: Southeast Asian GPU clouds have been a major source of rentable AI compute, and a licensing freeze could tighten capacity and raise prices for anyone training or serving models in the region.

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: Trump says a pardon for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is 'always an option'

stories.headline: Pentagon weighed Cold War law to get Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
stories.dek: Trump, who pressed Nvidia's board by phone, says a pardon for Huang is 'always an option' ahead of his December 1 congressional appearance.
stories.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his deputy Steve Feinberg discussed using the Defense Production Act to pressure Nvidia's board into reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, The Washington Post reports, according to Tom's Hardware. The 1950 law does not let a president install a CEO. One person familiar with the talks said it could instead force Nvidia to shift more production to military projects, hurting its profits and share price.

Huang resigned after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed employee who US intelligence officials believe passed Nvidia information to Chinese officials. The board reinstated him on November 23. Trump confirmed he called into a board meeting to push for his return.

Huang meets the House Foreign Affairs Committee on December 1. Asked about a pardon, Trump said: "It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." Nvidia's top lawyer faces questions on December 2.
key_points: The Washington Post reports Pentagon leaders considered the 1950 Defense Production Act to pressure Nvidia's board over Huang's return.
Nvidia reinstated Huang on November 23 after Trump publicly and privately pushed for it.
Trump says a pardon is "always an option" as Huang prepares for House Foreign Affairs Committee questions on December 1.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: OpenAI warns GPT-6.2 Astra will hit usage limits 40% faster because it fixed a bug

stories.headline: OpenAI fixes billing bug, GPT-6.2 Astra now burns limits 40% faster
stories.dek: A mistake had discounted Astra and Sol usage for most users; OpenAI is offering one banked usage reset as an apology.
stories.body:
OpenAI has fixed a billing bug that wrongly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage, and users will now hit their limits faster, BleepingComputer reports. "Comparing to last week, you will reach your limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol," Tibo Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, said in a post on X.

OpenAI says it won't charge users for the difference caused by the mistake. As an apology, it is adding one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro and Business plans. BleepingComputer confirmed the reset appears under ChatGPT Settings > Usage and expires after a month.

OpenAI says both models still use allowances more efficiently than their predecessors, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Other models keep their existing usage calculations.
key_points: GPT-6.2 Astra users will hit limits 40 percent faster than last week, and Sol users 25 percent faster.
Go, Plus, Pro and Business subscribers get one banked usage reset that expires after a month.
Only GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are affected; other models keep their existing usage calculations.

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: Electronics manufacturers set up memory 'war rooms' to find, lock in DRAM supplies amid worst shortage in history

stories.headline: Electronics makers open DRAM 'war rooms' as memory shortage deepens
stories.dek: Smaller firms scour eBay, call hundreds of brokers and risk the gray market while the big three chipmakers prioritize HBM for AI.
stories.body:
Electronics manufacturers, especially smaller ones, are setting up "procurement war rooms" to hunt for DRAM, Tom's Hardware reports, in what it calls the worst memory shortage in history. Staff search eBay and contact hundreds of brokers, snapping up batches as small as five or 12 units. Some turn to the gray market, where sellers reportedly mix used chips into new orders.

Citing The Wall Street Journal, the outlet says Taiwanese module maker Apacer took out loans to have cash ready if supply appears. "If chips show up, we take it," President Gibson Chen said.

Memory prices have climbed 500 percent as Micron, Samsung and SK hynix shift production to HBM for AI. SK hynix calls 2027 the "worst year" for shortages, and new fabs are not expected online until 2028.
key_points: Smaller electronics makers are buying DRAM via eBay, hundreds of brokers and the gray market, Tom's Hardware reports.
Memory prices have risen 500 percent as Micron, Samsung and SK hynix prioritize HBM for AI.
SK hynix expects 2027 to be the worst year; new factories are not expected to produce chips until 2028.

featured.body:
